title: Economics A: Microeconomics I
info: **Course:** 1,128 Economics A: Microeconomics I, Group 2, Dr. Magnus Hoffmann (5.5 ECTS): 12 lectures, 8 tutorials, independent study.

- **Textbook (TB):** Kolmar (2022), *Principles of Microeconomics*, 2nd ed. It complements the lectures but does not replace them. **Workbook (WB):** Kolmar & Hoffmann (2022), the basis of the tutorials.
- The textbook **Digressions** are the independent-study part and are tested in a **separate part of the final exam** (the Digressions guide says 36 of 180 points, 12 T/F questions).
- **Not exam-relevant:** TB chapters 7, 8, 10, 11 and pp. 370–372 (1st paragraph). A mock exam (2025 exam) is published on Canvas mid-semester.
- Your PDFs cover Parts **1.1, 1.2 and 2.1**. Parts 2.2, 3.1–3.4 will appear once you add their slides.

questions.question: Lukas can spend Saturday working (CHF 150), studying (value to him CHF 100) or skiing (value CHF 130). He chooses to study. His opportunity cost is…
questions.explanation: Next-best alternative forgone = working (CHF 150). Not the sum (280).

questions.question: Which proposition has no truth value?
questions.explanation: Normative propositions can only be justified or criticized.

questions.question: According to Popper, which theory is unscientific?
options: One that cannot be falsified under any empirically accessible condition
One that is based on a model
questions.explanation: Good theories must be falsifiable; a theory that can never fail empirically has no empirical content.

questions.question: Country A produces 1 car or 4 tonnes of wheat per worker; country B produces 1 car or 2 tonnes of wheat per worker. Which is correct?
options: A has a comparative advantage in both goods
A has a comparative advantage in wheat, B in cars
B has a comparative advantage in wheat
No gains from trade are possible
questions.explanation: OC of 1 car: A 4 t wheat, B 2 t → B has the comparative advantage in cars; A in wheat (OC ¼ car vs. ½).

questions.question: The infant-industry argument (List 1841) recommends…
options: temporary protection of young industries, then reducing protection
complete free trade from the start
specializing only along today's comparative advantage
questions.explanation: Protect → grow to global competitiveness → reduce protection.

questions.question: Carla demands x = 12 − 2p and Dario x = 6 − p. Market demand for 0 ≤ p < 6 is…
questions.explanation: Both buy for p < 6: (12 − 2p) + (6 − p) = 18 − 3p. Both demands hit zero at p = 6.

questions.question: Which statement about a quantity tax is correct?
options: The side that legally pays the tax always bears it
With perfectly inelastic demand there is no welfare loss
Taxes never reduce the traded quantity
With perfectly elastic demand consumers bear the whole tax
questions.explanation: Quantity is unchanged, so no trade is lost; consumers bear the tax. With perfectly elastic demand, producers bear it.

questions.question: Digression 3.3: money solves which problem of a barter economy?
questions.explanation: In barter, a trade needs both sides to want exactly what the other offers.

questions.question:
Demand x(p) = 120 − 2p, supply y(p) = p.
(a) Compute the equilibrium price and quantity. (b) Compute consumer surplus and producer surplus. (c) Compute the price elasticity of demand at the equilibrium and say whether demand is elastic or inelastic there.
questions.model:
(a) 120 − 2p = p → p* = 40, x* = 40.
(b) Inverse demand P(x) = 60 − x/2 (choke price 60); inverse supply Q(y) = y. CS = ½·40·(60 − 40) = 400. PS = ½·40·40 = 800.
(c) ε = (dx/dp)·(p/x) = −2·40/40 = −2 → |ε| > 1: elastic.

keyPoints.text: (b) CS = 400 (inverse demand / choke price 60 used correctly)
(c) ε = −2 and correctly classified as elastic

questions.question: Using the lecture's three questions about trade, explain why ‘gains from trade’ does not mean ‘everybody gains automatically’. Refer to at least two of the questions.
questions.model: Q1 (everybody better off?): no; specialization and trade can create losers, e.g. in sequential integration a partner is dropped and falls back to autarky; US data show gains were real but very unevenly distributed. Q2 (institutions needed?): yes; specialization creates interdependence and hold-up vulnerability (power asymmetries exploited by the more powerful partner), so gains depend on the rules of exchange; economics is ‘primarily the study of institutions’. Q3 (robust?): the mechanism is general, but comparative advantage is dynamic and can be shifted by investment or policy (List; Juhász 2018).

keyPoints.text: Q1: trade can create losers, with a mechanism or evidence (sequential integration / US income data)
Q2: hold-up problem / dependency, so institutions (rules) are needed
Q3: comparative advantage is dynamic (List or Juhász), or a second question developed with correct concepts
